http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/06/north.text: North Korea fired at least one ballistic missile over the Sea of Japan on Thursday, Seoul's military said, after Pyongyang lambasted Tokyo for beefing up its military stance in the Pacific."Our military detected a short-range ballistic missile launched from the Wonsan area of North Korea at around 5:00 pm," South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) said in a message to news organisations.The JCS said earlier the missile was launched towards the East Sea, referring to the body of water also known as the Sea of Japan.Japan's defence ministry also posted on X that "something that may be a ballistic missile has been launched from North Korea."A separate post shortly afterwards said "there is no longer any impact on the areas around Japan."Seoul has strengthened surveillance and maintained readiness for possible additional launches while sharing information with its security allies, the United States and Japan, the JCS said.North Korea has repeatedly declared itself an "irreversible" nuclear state since leader Kim Jong- un's 2019 summit with US President Donald Trump collapsed over the scope of denuclearisation and sanctions relief.Tokyo's Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said earlier this week that Japan's military needs to be boosted with a "sense of urgency and crisis," as a new government assessment warned of growing threats from China, Russia and North Korea.In a statement carried by North Korean state media on Wednesday, Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of leader Kim Jong-un, said Pyongyang's "leadership will set up additional military options which are obviously due to Japan's transformation."'New militarism'North Korea has recently deepened economic and military ties with Russia, supplying troops and munitions for Moscow's war in Ukraine in exchange for financial support, food, energy and military technology, analysts say.It has also repeatedly branded Seoul, a security ally of Washington, its "most hostile" enemy.Japan's defence ministry declined to comment directly on Kim Yo-jong's Wednesday diatribe but said the country's defence capabilities "remain bare minimum" and "are not meant to threaten other countries.""Ours isn't the defence meant to wage wars, but to prevent new wars, strictly kept to self-defence and within the scope of our (pacifist) Constitution and international laws," it said in a statement.Tokyo raised its military expenditure by 9.7% to $62.2 billion (€53.8 billion) in 2025, equivalent to 1.4% of GDP, its highest share since 1958.China, a key ally of North Korea, has also recently expressed alarm at what it sees as "new militarism" by Japan.South Korea's dovish President Lee Jae Myung has reversed the stance of his hawkish predecessor since taking power in Seoul in June 2025, offering nuclear-armed Pyongyang talks without preconditions.The hermetic leadership of North Korea has yet to respond to his repeated offers.The two Koreas remain technically at war because their 1950-53 conflict ended with an armistice rather than a peace treaty.

https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/mag.text: World War II was a time when letters were often the only regular connection between American servicemen overseas and the people waiting for them at home. There were no text messages or video calls, so soldiers wrote about almost everything, from bad food and long days to fear, loneliness and the people they missed. For Louis “Speedy” Weber, a young New Yorker who went to war in 1942, those letters became a record of his marriage to Frances. More than 300 survived, and decades later they would help solve a family mystery that had lasted for years.Weber was 23 when he enlisted in June 1942, while Frances was 24. According to government records cited by The Washington Post, they had been married for about a year and lived in the Bronx.Weber's first wartime letter was written on June 9, the same day he joined the Army. He was still eating at an Italian restaurant when he wrote to Frances that he was being sent to Fort Dix in New Jersey.The letters continued once he reached training camp. Army life was tiring and unfamiliar, and Weber wrote about getting up early, kitchen duty and military rules.“I don’t know whether they want to make men of us or kill us before we get to Japan,” he wrote in one of his first letters, according to The Washington Post.A week later, he admitted that being kept busy was actually helping him cope with being away from home.“I don’t feel as blue as I did yesterday,” he wrote. “Things are beginning to shape up and they don’t give me a minute to think about anything but Army life, and in a way that’s the best thing for me, because if I stopped to think about home I’d go nuts.”Hundreds of letters followed him through the warWeber eventually went overseas and served with Army engineer units in North Africa and Europe. His letters travelled from places including Sicily, France, Belgium and Germany back to Frances' home on Jesup Avenue in the Bronx.The correspondence was not always serious. Weber asked for food and supplies from home, including salami, sardines, Ritz crackers and chewing gum. He also teased Frances and wrote openly about how much he missed her.USO archivist Michael Case told Smithsonian that Weber came across as an ordinary young man who was simply trying to get through the war while remaining close to his wife.“He’s an everyday guy, not a general, no one famous, just doing his job and loving and being emotional and screwing up occasionally,” Case said.Case also found Weber's writing unusually expressive despite its simple language. He described it as “everyday elegant.”Weber often ended his letters with the same affectionate line: “You are always in my heart.”He witnessed the D-Day invasionSome of the most important letters were written in 1944, when Weber took part in the Allied invasion of Normandy.In a letter written shortly after D-Day, he tried to explain to Frances just how enormous the operation had been.“This invasion made my other invasions look feeble,” he wrote. “I never before saw as many ships, airplanes, and equipment in my whole war time experience.”He also described looking toward the sky and barely being able to see the sun because of the Allied aircraft.“I had a hard time seeing the sun, because of the planes we had up there. It was a sight I’ll never forget,” Weber wrote.The letters continued through the Battle of the Bulge and the final months of the war. In May 1945, Weber wrote from Czechoslovakia with news that he would not have to continue into the Pacific because of his previous campaigns.“Baby thats the best news I’ve heard in three years of Army life,” he told Frances.Soon, after three years apart, he would be going home.133327651The letters disappear for decadesWeber survived the war and returned to Frances. The couple remained married for the rest of their lives, but surprisingly little was known about what happened to them afterward.According to The Washington Post, Weber died in Florida in 1997 at 78, while Frances died in 2005 at 87. They were buried next to each other near Fort Lauderdale.Their letters, meanwhile, survived somewhere.In 2022, an anonymous donor gave more than 300 of them to the USO. The collection eventually reached Case at the organization's headquarters in Arlington, Virginia. The USO said the letters had been preserved for decades before being opened to the public.The identity of the person who donated them remained unknown.The USO searches for Speedy's familyThe letters immediately raised another question: who were Speedy and Frances, and did anyone in their family still know them?The USO tried to find relatives and in 2024 contacted The Washington Post. The newspaper's reporting established more details about the couple's early lives, including that their families lived only a few blocks apart in New York in 1940.But the trail largely stopped there.The USO later digitized 26 letters and published photographs and transcriptions online. The collection was also promoted alongside Pressure, a World War II film about the tense days before D-Day, with actor Andrew Scott reading one of Weber's letters for a USO video.Jennifer Passey, the USO's vice president of communications, told The Washington Post in May 2026: “We’re putting the letters back out there as people are talking about this movie. We would love for anyone who may know more about Speedy or his wife, Frances, to reach out to us.”That appeal finally worked.133327669An amateur genealogist finds the missing linkAfter the May 2026 Washington Post story, California amateur genealogist Matthew Brown began searching genealogy records. According to the newspaper's later account, he spent several hours building a family tree and eventually found a possible living relative, Arthur Serota.Serota turned out to be Weber's nephew.He remembered Speedy as a warm and generous uncle and was able to provide researchers with information about the couple that had been missing from the record. Another niece, Karen Weber Figilis, also came forward with memories and family photographs.For the family, the discovery offered a different way of looking at Speedy and Frances. The letters were no longer simply old wartime documents. They were the beginning of their marriage, written at a time when the couple had almost no idea what the next few years would bring.Serota told The Washington Post that reading the letters made him think differently about his uncle's marriage.“To me they hit the lottery. To have a love affair last a lifetime, it doesn’t get better than that,” he said.The mystery of who originally donated the letters has still not been solved. But after more than 80 years, the letters have done something almost as important: they brought Speedy and Frances' story back to the family that had nearly lost it.Why letters mattered so much during World War IIFor American troops serving overseas, mail was not just a way of passing time. The National Postal Museum notes that letters were considered extremely important to military morale because they helped soldiers maintain a connection with ordinary life back home. Families were encouraged to write about daily routines, local news and even small things happening at home, since those details could make the distance feel a little less overwhelming.The amount of correspondence moving during the war became enormous. In 1944, a survey by the Post Office Department found that the 11.5 million men and women serving in the military were sending an average of 6.04 pieces of mail every week. That meant military postal services had to move an extraordinary amount of paper across the world while also making room on ships and aircraft for weapons, food and other supplies.To reduce the amount of cargo space taken up by letters, the military expanded the use of V-Mail, short for Victory Mail. Instead of transporting the original letter, specially designed sheets were photographed onto 16mm microfilm and sent overseas. The images were then enlarged and printed near their destination. The system allowed a huge amount of correspondence to be moved in a much smaller space.

Independent MP Monique Ryan says she supports more resources to secure offices. ‘If it makes my team feel better and safer to have bollards out the front, I’m happy.’ Photograph: Martin Keep/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Floral tributes outside the Helen Haines’s office in Wangaratta. Independent MP Monique Ryan says she supports more resources to secure offices. ‘If it makes my team feel better and safer to have bollards out the front, I’m happy.’ Photograph: Martin Keep/AFP/Getty Images Helen Haines Australian politicians say they are paying thousands for their own security upgrades amid rising threats Home and office safety a common concern in Australian federal police and Asio safety briefings with politicians following alleged attack on MP Helen Haines Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast Josh Butler and Krishani Dhanji Wed 21 Oct 2026 10.00 EDT Last modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 10.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Security agencies will review safety precautions for MPs’ homes and offices after numerous federal politicians told police and Asio in safety briefings that they were worried about widening threats after the alleged attack on Helen Haines . The Labor government and politicians across the parliament are still considering how they will respond when they return to Canberra next week, with ideas being floated including a new committee on MPs’ safety, greater resources for police, and motions of condolence for Haines, who lost both her legs after Monday’s incident . Renewed calls from the crossbench for reforms to question time and the tone of debate in parliament are unlikely to be taken up by the major parties. In safety briefings with the Australian federal police and Asio granted to Labor, Coalition and crossbench MPs on Wednesday, security of homes and electorate offices was a common concern, according to Guardian Australia interviews with 10 MPs. While a broad review of safety and security is unlikely at this stage, multiple MPs across the political spectrum told Guardian Australia they had spent thousands of dollars of their own money to install safety features based on the advice of the federal police. Politicians say more security would ‘let bad people win’ after alleged attack on Helen Haines: ‘We don’t want to be locked off’ Read more Federal ministers receive stronger security assistance, but numerous backbenchers said they felt under-resourced, saying many angry constituents may see all politicians as a homogenous group, and may not differentiate between cabinet members and ordinary local MPs. “People are getting activated now because they see us as part of the government. We represent the system to them, as much as anyone else,” independent Monique Ryan said. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here Two years ago, the AFP recorded 951 reports of harassing and threatening behaviour against office holders. Last year, that increased to 1,067. On Wednesday, police arrested a man after he allegedly caused a disturbance at a Perth electorate office and was reported to have made verbal threats “while in possession of what has been described as nunchucks”. No one was injured as a result, Western Australia police said. ‘Not well protected’ A number of politicians asked to speak anonymously to discuss reflections from the briefings. While many praised the AFP’s response when their staff contacted them – for instance, to seek advice on holding public events – some said they had received less timely assistance from local police when they requested help, such as to respond to aggressive visitors. Numerous MPs said they did not want security guards or armed escorts for themselves in public , but that they felt alarmed for the safety of their homes and families. Some said they would feel more comfortable with cameras and floodlights at home, and had decided to pay for their own upgrades after not being offered such features in risk assessments conducted by security agencies. One independent MP said crossbenchers questioned whether extra home security features should be paid for by the public. Several MPs said they wanted more security and safety support, but questioned how much impact that would have on their overall safety and how much more the AFP could do. Helen Haines has lost both legs but ‘heart and mind are in good shape’, husband says – video Guardian Australia was told security officials had committed to assessing safety settings of MPs who raised specific concerns. While a broad-ranging government review is at this stage not expected, other responses could include giving MPs more information on the background work that policing agencies conduct year-round, such as threat assessments and periodic checks. The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, told News24 his government had overseen “an increase in funding for security for members of parliament in the last couple of years”. “We want to make sure that people can feel as much comfort as possible, that everything’s being done to maximise security. But also, I think parliamentarians across the board are determined to make sure we can continue to engage as we need to in this great democracy of ours,” he said. A spokesperson for the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, said: “Reviews of the threats faced by high office holders are constantly conducted by our agencies.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Politics, really Our political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for you after newsletter promotion Ryan, who is close with Haines, said she had rarely discussed safety arrangements with fellow MPs until recent times, but claimed many colleagues were “now realising they’re having common experiences”. She was supportive of a broader review into safety, and more resources to secure offices. “If it makes my team feel better and safer to have bollards out the front, I’m happy,” she said. Two Labor MPs said some government backbenchers had expressed frustrations towards the finance department for not adequately funding safety measures for their electorate offices or doing so in a timely way. One said money was “always an issue” with the department, and expected more MPs to be directly lobbying the prime minister to improve office security. Graph of threats to politicians increasing Nationals MP Sam Birrell, whose electorate neighbours Haines’s in Indi, said regional politicians had particular concerns, with many being highly visible in their communities and locals often knowing where they lived. “Some of the MPs were frustrated there’s not clear advice on things like whether to advertise mobile offices or have signs on cars,” he said. “There were some complaints about whether people are able to get fairly modest security measures … that needs to be reviewed.” Multiple people across meetings raised concerns about how to protect electorate office staff. Liberal senator James Paterson told Radio National electorate offices were “very exposed” and were “not well protected”. Asio and AFP have been contacted for comment.
